title: Is Raising Your Voice An Effective Classroom Management Strategy? m-management-strategy/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Michael Linsin argues that raising one's voice, though common in schools and effective at producing immediate compliance, is a serious mistake for classroom management. He lays out five specific harms: it damages the teacher-student relationship by creating an adversarial dynamic, it loses effectiveness over time and forces teachers to escalate further, it models emotional reactivity that students then imitate with each other, it opens teachers to complaints from parents and administrators, and it worsens overall behavior even as it curbs misbehavior in the moment. Linsin acknowledges that raised volume has its place during energetic lessons, storytelling, or safety concerns, but not during discipline. His prescribed alternative is a calm, quiet, steady voice paired with consistent reliance on a classroom management plan. The piece is written in his signature direct, aphoristic style, building a case through repeated short claims before landing on a practical recommendation.
points: Raising your voice produces short-term compliance but damages the teacher-student relationship, replacing respect and rapport with intimidation.
Voice escalation has diminishing returns over time, requiring ever-louder and more aggressive tactics to achieve the same effect.
Emotional reactions from teachers model complaining and disrespect, which students then mirror toward each other and the teacher.
Habitual yelling exposes teachers to parent and administrator complaints that are difficult to defend because the conflict became personal.
The recommended alternative is a soft, clear, steady voice combined with consistent enforcement of a classroom management plan, reserving louder volume for engaging lessons or safety needs.
quotes: When you raise your voice loud enough to startle or alarm students, you’re rewarded with immediate attention and compliance.
Although it can indeed stop students in their tracks, which is why it’s so prevalent, raising your voice is a monumental mistake.
Yelling, shouting, barking orders, and the like is antagonistic. It creates a you-against-them relationship rather than one grounded in respect and rapport.
Raising your voice has a diminishing effect. The more you use it with the same group of students, the less effective it becomes.
Reacting emotionally to misbehavior provides a terrible role model for your students. It teaches them to complain and stomp their feet when things don’t go their way.
When you use fearful, loud, or startling tactics, it may indeed curb misbehavior in the moment, but it increases misbehavior overall.
It’s best to stand in one place and speak just loud enough to be heard.
